creativityHighWhatItMeans:
Creativity is a default mode, not something switched on only when asked — new angles show up unprompted, in routine work as much as big projects
Constraints (tight budget, short deadline, limited people) tend to sharpen thinking rather than shut it down
Comfortable holding multiple possible approaches at once instead of collapsing quickly to "the" answer
Genuinely energized by ambiguous or undefined problems, where the first step isn't obvious
creativityHighStrengths:
Regularly reframes problems and offers alternative approaches instead of defaulting to the first idea
Turns constraints into fuel — creative output often increases, not decreases, under real limits
A strong brainstorming partner who unblocks teams stuck on a single approach
Spots non-obvious connections between unrelated ideas, people, or projects
creativityHighConsiderations:
Setting a hard stop for idea generation, so exploration doesn't quietly replace a decision that needs to get made
Noticing when interest fades once a project moves from "figuring it out" to repetitive execution — and building in accountability for the finish, not just the start
Checking the team's actual pace before introducing another new idea; more options aren't always useful mid-execution
Pairing with someone execution-minded (or deliberately building execution habits) so good ideas don't stall before they ship
creativityLowWhatItMeans:
Reaches for known, proven approaches first, and generally sees that as the responsible choice rather than a limitation
Generates a new idea when the situation calls for one, but it isn't a running habit
More comfortable executing a clear plan than sitting in an undefined, ambiguous problem
Trusts what's already been tested over what's merely interesting
creativityLowStrengths:
Reliable, low-risk execution — sticks with approaches that are known to work
Filters out impractical ideas quickly; stays grounded in what's realistic
Predictable to work with, and doesn't introduce unnecessary change
Keeps a team focused rather than chasing every new idea that comes up
creativityLowConsiderations:
Building a habit of asking "is there a different way to do this" before defaulting to the familiar approach, even when the familiar one seems to be working
Creating space for the team to float alternative ideas without it feeling like second-guessing the plan
Noticing early when a standard playbook stops fitting a situation, rather than after it's clearly failed
Borrowing creative thinking deliberately — a second opinion, a structured brainstorm, someone whose default mode is generating options
eqHighWhatItMeans:
Reads emotional cues — tone, body language, what's not being said — in real time, including in tense or high-stakes moments
Regulates their own reactions under pressure rather than being visibly rattled by them
Adjusts approach based on how a message is likely to land for a specific person, not just its content
Notices when someone on the team is struggling before it's announced
eqHighStrengths:
Builds trust quickly — people feel heard and understood
Reads the room and adjusts approach in most situations, including tense ones
Effective at defusing conflict before it escalates
Gets more honest, complete information from people because they feel safe bringing it
eqHighConsiderations:
Noticing when emotional investment is slowing down a decision that needs to be made quickly and cleanly
Practicing directness — delivering a hard message clearly, without over-cushioning it to protect the other person's feelings
Setting boundaries around absorbing other people's stress, so it doesn't become a personal cost
Watching for a bias toward harmony over necessary conflict, especially in decisions with a clear right answer
eqLowWhatItMeans:
Evaluates situations primarily on facts and outcomes, with less attention to the emotional undercurrent in the room
Notices emotional cues mainly when they're pointed out directly or the setting is calm, not automatically
Tends to treat "how people feel about it" as separate from "what's the right call"
Can be personally difficult to read, even when not intending to be
eqLowStrengths:
Stays task-focused and unaffected by emotional noise in the room
Makes decisions without being swayed by how people will feel about them
Steady under conditions that would rattle a more emotionally reactive leader
Doesn't personalize conflict or take feedback as an attack
eqLowConsiderations:
Building a habit of checking in on how a decision landed, not just whether it was correct
Naming feelings explicitly when they come up, since they often won't be inferred without being said
Asking directly how someone is doing, especially before or after a high-stress period, rather than assuming things are fine because nothing was said
Watching for trust eroding quietly — it often shows up as people going around a leader rather than to them
visionHighWhatItMeans:
Holds a clear picture of where things are headed and returns to it often, not just at kickoff meetings or annual planning
Naturally connects today's decisions back to a longer-term direction
Communicates the "why" behind the work in a way that gives people something to orient around during uncertainty
Thinks in terms of where the team/business needs to be in a year or more, not just this quarter
visionHighStrengths:
Anchors the team during ambiguity with a clear sense of where things are headed
Vision consistently shapes day-to-day decisions, not just big-picture ones
Exceptional at aligning people around a future state they can't yet see
Gives people a reason to push through short-term friction because the destination is clear
visionHighConsiderations:
Checking in on present-day problems that are easy to wave past in service of the bigger story — a real complaint today deserves a real answer today
Translating the vision into concrete near-term steps for people who need something tangible, not just direction
Staying close enough to daily operations that the vision doesn't start to feel disconnected from what the team is actually experiencing
Confirming that managers and team members are actually aligned with the stated direction, rather than assuming buy-in because the vision has been communicated
visionLowWhatItMeans:
Oriented toward what's happening right now — today's problems, this week's priorities — more than a multi-year direction
Can state a goal or direction when asked, but it doesn't come up unprompted in day-to-day decisions
More comfortable executing within a direction someone else has set than generating that direction
Judges progress by what got done, not by how it connects to a longer-term story
visionLowStrengths:
Highly responsive to what's actually happening day-to-day
Doesn't get distracted by abstract future-state thinking when there's real work in front of them
Comfortable letting others supply the "why" while focusing on the "what"
Keeps plans grounded in present reality instead of over-indexing on a future that may not play out as imagined
visionLowConsiderations:
Naming a direction out loud, even a simple one, so the team has something to orient around beyond this week's task list
Noticing when the team seems to be drifting or losing motivation — that's often a signal that a "why" is missing, not just a "what"
Revisiting stated goals regularly rather than only when directly asked, so they actually stick
Partnering with someone vision-oriented, or deliberately blocking time to think beyond the immediate horizon
influenceHighWhatItMeans:
Moves people to act, agree, or change their mind regardless of formal title or authority
Adjusts the pitch depending on the audience — what lands with one group won't necessarily land with another, and that's accounted for
Comfortable building support before a decision is made official, not just announcing it afterward
Reads what actually matters to a given person or group and leads with that, rather than a one-size-fits-all argument
influenceHighStrengths:
Earns buy-in across audiences without needing to lean on formal authority
Mobilizes people effectively, including cross-functionally
Builds coalitions and gets people moving in the same direction
Turns a good idea into something people will actually champion, not just tolerate
influenceHighConsiderations:
Checking that an idea has been fully vetted before selling it hard — persuasiveness can outrun the underlying substance if it isn't
Making room for quieter voices in the room rather than letting natural presence dominate the conversation
Being transparent about the ask, rather than relying on charisma to smooth over a case that hasn't been made explicit
Noticing when "getting buy-in" starts to matter more than whether the decision itself is the right one
influenceLowWhatItMeans:
Relies on position, facts, or established relationships to move people, rather than persuasion as a practiced skill
Effective one-on-one or in small, familiar groups, less so scaling that to a room of strangers
States a case plainly and lets it stand on its own merits rather than building a deliberate pitch
Doesn't naturally reach for storytelling or framing to make an argument land
influenceLowStrengths:
Straightforward — doesn't rely on manipulation or persuasion tactics to get buy-in
Effective in close, familiar relationships where trust is already established
What they say is what they mean; no hidden agenda in how they influence
Earns durable trust precisely because they aren't seen as "working" people
influenceLowConsiderations:
Practicing framing a case for a specific audience rather than presenting it the same way regardless of who's listening
Speaking up earlier and more often in group settings, where quieter voices are easy to lose
Building relationships beyond the immediate circle, since influence without an existing relationship is a learnable skill, not a fixed trait
Recognizing that being right isn't the same as being convincing — a good idea still needs a case made for it
executionHighWhatItMeans:
Turns plans into finished outcomes reliably, including when volume or pressure picks up
Has systems and habits (not just willpower) that keep work moving even when things get busy
Treats a plan as something to be delivered, not just discussed
Tracks follow-through closely — commitments made are commitments tracked to completion
executionHighStrengths:
Exceptionally dependable — consistent output even under high volume or pressure
Systems and habits hold up when things get busy, not just when conditions are calm
Reliably turns vague goals into concrete next steps
Gives a team confidence that what gets committed to actually gets delivered
executionHighConsiderations:
Building in a deliberate checkpoint to ask "is this still the right plan," rather than pushing through momentum alone
Making space for creative input mid-execution instead of treating the plan as fixed once it's in motion
Watching for process becoming the priority over the people or outcomes it's meant to serve
Noticing when a plan needs to break — persistence is a strength until it's protecting a decision that's already wrong
executionLowWhatItMeans:
Plans and good intentions don't reliably turn into finished outcomes, especially once real pressure or volume shows up
Follow-through tends to hold up when conditions are calm and falls off when things get busy
Comfortable abandoning an approach that isn't working, sometimes before giving it a full chance to
Tends to rely on motivation in the moment rather than systems that carry the work when motivation dips
executionLowStrengths:
Comfortable pivoting away from a plan that isn't working
Doesn't get overly attached to a single approach or process
Open to changing direction without much friction
Quick to recognize when something genuinely isn't working, rather than pushing through out of stubbornness
executionLowConsiderations:
Building a simple system (even a basic one — a checklist, a weekly review) rather than relying on remembering everything
Committing to fewer things at once, so what does get committed to has a real chance of being finished
Noticing the pattern of abandoning a plan under pressure specifically, and building in extra structure for exactly those moments
Separating "this isn't working" from "this is hard" before deciding to change direction
adaptabilityHighWhatItMeans:
Adjusts quickly when plans, information, or circumstances change, without needing much recovery time
Functions well with incomplete information rather than waiting for full certainty before acting
Treats disruption as a normal condition to work within, not an emergency
Comfortable holding a loose plan that's expected to change, rather than a fixed one
adaptabilityHighStrengths:
Thrives in flux — setbacks barely slow them down
Functions well under ambiguity and incomplete information
Steadies the team during disruption instead of adding to it
Recovers quickly from a plan not working out, without losing momentum
adaptabilityHighConsiderations:
Giving a new direction time to actually work before moving to the next one — not every plan needs a pivot
Communicating changes clearly enough that the rest of the team can track what's current, since what's obvious to a highly adaptable leader isn't always obvious to others
Watching for a pattern of the newest idea always looking better than the one already in motion
Building in occasional stability on purpose, even when it isn't strictly necessary, so the team has something steady to hold onto
adaptabilityLowWhatItMeans:
Prefers stability and clear rules — a well-defined process feels safer and more reliable than an open-ended one
Change, especially unplanned change, is genuinely disruptive rather than a minor adjustment
Needs more time and information than a highly adaptable leader before feeling ready to shift direction
Builds real depth by staying with an approach long enough to master it, rather than moving on quickly
adaptabilityLowStrengths:
Brings real consistency and deep expertise within a stable lane
Predictable — people know what they're going to get
Strong when the environment doesn't require constant change
Sees a plan through rather than abandoning it at the first sign of difficulty
adaptabilityLowConsiderations:
Practicing making a decision with incomplete information on lower-stakes situations, to build comfort before it's forced by a real crisis
Naming the discomfort of a needed change directly, rather than delaying it while waiting to feel more ready
Building a small "what if this changes" contingency into plans upfront, so a shift doesn't require starting over
Noticing the cost of staying the course too long — sometimes the harder call is the more adaptable one
